content: CDON, also known as Cell adhesion molecule-related/down-regulated by oncogenes, is a protein encoded by the CDON gene in humans. CDON and BOC are cell surface receptors that belong to the immunoglobulin (Ig)/fibronectin type III (FNIII) repeat family. These receptors are involved in the process of myogenic differentiation. Both CDON and BOC are co-expressed during development, form complexes with each other in a cis manner, and share similarities in their ectodomains. However, each receptor has a distinct and unique long cytoplasmic tail. CDON is a conserved transmembrane glycoprotein that is part of a subgroup within the immunoglobulin superfamily of cell adhesion molecules. It is expressed in proliferating and differentiating myoblast cell lines, and evidence suggests that it plays a critical role in mediating cell–cell interactions between muscle precursor cells, which are essential for myogenesis. Additionally, CDON is expressed in neural crest precursor cells, where it regulates the localization of N-cadherin, providing a mechanism for directed neural crest migration. The CDON protein has been shown to bind to all three mammalian isoforms of Hedgehog proteins: Sonic Hedgehog (Shh), Indian Hedgehog (Ihh), and Desert Hedgehog (Dhh). Mutations in the CDON gene are believed to reduce the activity of the Sonic Hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway, which is crucial for stimulating cell proliferation, differentiation, and tissue patterning during various stages of animal development. CDON has been implicated in the differentiation of midbrain dopaminergic neurons through its interaction with the Shh signaling pathway. Mutations in the CDON gene have also been associated with holoprosencephaly, a structural brain anomaly in which the developing forebrain fails to properly separate into right and left hemispheres. Furthermore, CDON mutations can synergistically interact with prenatal alcohol exposure, increasing susceptibility to holoprosencephaly. Gene knockdown studies have provided additional insights into CDON's role. In zebrafish, CDON knockdown using morpholinos altered eye development. In chick embryos, CDON was shown to be important for restricting the size of the optic stalk and ventral retina. Double CDON knockout mice exhibit optic nerve hypoplasia (ONH), a prominent feature of septo-optic dysplasia (SOD), which is also observed in mice prenatally exposed to ethanol. CDON-deficient animals also display cardiac dysfunction characterized by increased fibrosis, with these cardiac effects being mediated through hyperactivation of the WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway. CDON has been shown to interact with CDH1 (E-cadherin) and BOC, further highlighting its role in cellular signaling and developmental processes.
